title: What are Virtual Threads, what problem do they solve (cheap blocking for I/O-bound), when do they NOT help (CPU-bound), and what is thread pinning?
keyPoints: Virtual threads are lightweight, JVM-managed threads that cost roughly 1 KB each instead of the 1 MB a platform thread requires
When a virtual thread blocks on I/O the JVM unmounts it from its carrier and mounts another, so the carrier is never idle
They solve the C10K problem by allowing millions of concurrent threads for I/O-bound workloads
They do NOT speed up CPU-bound work because the carrier stays occupied during computation
Thread pinning occurs inside synchronized blocks or JNI calls where the virtual thread cannot unmount
Use Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() for the standard one-thread-per-task model
In Spring Boot set spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true to make all request-handling threads virtual

s1_definition.oneliner: A virtual thread is a lightweight, JVM-managed thread that unmounts from its carrier OS thread when it blocks on I/O, enabling millions of concurrent threads at roughly 1 KB each.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Virtual thread** – a thread managed entirely by the JVM, not by the operating system, introduced as final in Java 21 via JEP 444.
- **Carrier thread** – the platform (OS) thread on which a virtual thread is mounted for execution; the JVM maintains a small pool of carriers.
- **Unmounting** – when a virtual thread blocks on I/O (database call, HTTP request, file read), the JVM detaches it from its carrier so the carrier can run another virtual thread.
- **Cost** – each virtual thread uses roughly 1 KB of stack space versus roughly 1 MB for a platform thread, so millions can coexist.
- **Limitation** – virtual threads do not help CPU-bound tasks because the carrier stays occupied during computation, and thread pinning inside `synchronized` blocks prevents unmounting.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a bank with 20 teller counters (carrier threads) and an unlimited supply of numbered tokens (virtual threads). Each customer takes a token and waits. When a teller finishes one customer and that customer leaves to get a document (I/O block), the teller immediately calls the next token instead of sitting idle. One teller can serve hundreds of customers in a day because most of the time customers are away fetching documents. But if a customer needs the teller to perform a long manual calculation (CPU-bound), the teller is fully occupied and cannot switch.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Virtual threads are the most significant concurrency feature Java has added since the original threading model. They are lightweight, JVM-managed threads that cost roughly 1 KB each instead of the 1 MB that a platform thread requires. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it from its carrier OS thread and mounts another virtual thread, so the carrier is never idle. This means you can have millions of virtual threads running concurrently on a handful of carrier threads.

The key insight is that virtual threads make blocking cheap. Before Java 21, writing scalable I/O-bound servers meant either limiting concurrency with thread pools (and queuing excess requests) or adopting reactive programming with its complex callback chains. Virtual threads let you write simple, synchronous, blocking code that scales to hundreds of thousands of concurrent connections. The programming model stays familiar: you call `jdbcTemplate.query(...)` or `httpClient.send(...)` and the runtime handles the efficiency.

Virtual threads do not help CPU-bound workloads. If a thread is computing a risk model or encrypting data, there is no I/O block for the JVM to exploit. The carrier stays occupied. For CPU-bound tasks, use a fixed-size platform thread pool sized to the number of CPU cores. Thread pinning is the other limitation: blocking inside a `synchronized` block or a JNI call prevents the virtual thread from unmounting. Replace `synchronized` with `ReentrantLock` on I/O paths.

In a banking system like National Bank of India, a transfer service handling 50,000 concurrent requests gives each request its own virtual thread. Each thread blocks on a database call and a fraud-check HTTP call. The eight carrier threads stay busy because whenever one virtual thread blocks, another is mounted immediately. The result is the throughput of a reactive system with the readability of imperative code.

Remember one sentence: virtual threads make blocking I/O cheap by unmounting from the carrier on every block, enabling millions of concurrent threads at 1 KB each.
